eyebrow: Eval round 2 · Save My Eyes · 3 runs per arm
h1: Does the copywriting skill change what an agent writes?
sub: Six unsupervised instances rewrote the Settings labels and the long-break ideas of Save My Eyes and wrote a headline. Three had the copywriting skill with its new interface-text reference. Three did not.

verdict.head: The slider label keeps its meaning: 3 of 3 with the skill, 0 of 3 without
verdict.body: Every skill run still says what is being delayed: breaks. Every baseline run dropped it, the same failure as round one.

verdict.head: The skill arm leaves passing text alone
verdict.body: Baseline runs changed 16 to 17 settings strings each, including a button, a notice title, the credits and a helper text nobody asked about. Skill runs changed 10 to 13 and none of those.

verdict.head: The baseline caught one accuracy issue more often
verdict.body: The first slider sets the gap between all breaks, not only short ones. 3 of 3 baseline runs fixed that. Only 1 of 3 skill runs did.

verdict.head: Verbs and house style survive with the skill
verdict.body: The sound switch kept its verb in 3 of 3 skill runs against 1 of 3. Skill runs kept the ideas' no-period style and roughly their length; baseline ideas grew about 30% and gained periods the short-break ideas do not have.

verdict.head: Headlines: safer and more uniform with the skill
verdict.body: All three skill headlines share one shape built on the default numbers and the screen cover. The baseline ranged wider, including one promise that only holds after a switch is turned on.

verdict.head: Small sample, and the baseline was not skill-free
verdict.body: Three runs per arm is enough to see a pattern, not to measure one. Two of the three baseline runs invoked the installed design:ux-copy skill on their own.

focus.title: The label that started this: “Pause breaks after a call ends”
focus.lede: In round one both arms shortened it into a vague noun phrase. The skill now carries an interface-text reference with a keep-every-slot rule. Each rewrite below is checked for the three things a reader needs, plus whether it matches what the code covers.
focus.truth: After a calendar meeting or a call ends, the app keeps holding a due break for this many more minutes. At zero the break starts right away.
focus.after: All six runs saw in the code that the wait also applies after calendar meetings, and said so. The difference is the object: no baseline run says what waits, every skill run does. Baseline run 3 also reads as a noun (“Delay: None”). Between “Hold breaks after a meeting or call ends” with “Off” at zero and “Delay the break after a meeting or call” with “No delay”, the choice is yours; both keep every slot.

SharedStrings.shortEvery.name: Slider: time between breaks
SharedStrings.shortEvery.ctx: value shown next to it: 20 min.
SharedStrings.shortEvery.note: The code uses this value as the gap before every break, and every third break is long. All three baseline runs corrected “short”; one skill run did, one kept the label, one reworded it but kept “short”. A point for the baseline, although two of its three versions lost the verb.

Skill runs 2 and 3 then use that same verb, Hold, on the slider below; skill run 1 chose Pause here and Delay there on purpose. Baseline runs all switch verb between the switches and the slider (Hold then Wait, Hold then Delay, Delay then Wait).

MenuSettingsPane.callsDetail.note: Not a label, and already clear. All three baseline runs rewrote it. All three skill runs left it.

SharedStrings.soundUi.note: All six runs found in the code when the sound plays and said it. The skill arm kept the verb in 3 of 3 (“Play a sound…”); the baseline in 1 of 3.

SharedStrings.fixing.note: The task was the Settings labels. Baseline runs also reworded this notice (2 runs), the Revert button (1) and the credits line (1). No skill run touched any of them.

headline.title: Headline for the app
headline.lede: Each instance got only a general description of the app, was told to read the code, and was kept away from the README and the product docs.
headline.note: The three skill runs converged on one shape: a number from the default settings, the mechanism (the screen gets covered) and the benefit. Every claim in them holds with default settings. The baseline varied more: one tight line, one that promises something that is off by default, one with no number. For range to pick from, the baseline gave more. For a line that is safe to ship unreviewed, the skill arm did.

headline_notes.base-1: 9 words. Built on the default interval and break length.
headline_notes.base-2: 15 words. The second half is only true once the user turns on a switch that is off by default; the run said so itself.
headline_notes.base-3: 13 words. Names the mechanism, but “every so often” gives no number.
headline_notes.skill-1: 16 words. Default numbers plus the mechanism; “actually” gives it an edge.
headline_notes.skill-2: 15 words. Same shape; “covers itself” is slightly odd.
headline_notes.skill-3: 13 words. Same shape without the break length.

score.title: Run by run
score.lede: Counts come from each worktree's diff against master.

method: Six fresh instances on the same model and effort, each in its own detached worktree of save-my-eyes at e82f144, the latest master on GitHub. The prompt was identical; the skill arm additionally loaded the copywriting skill by reading its files, because the installed plugin does not include it yet.
Each instance did all three tasks in one go, so one task may have coloured the next inside an instance.
Instances were told to learn the app from the Swift sources and not to read the README, PRODUCT.md, DESIGN.md or docs.
Everything shown comes from the git diff of each worktree. The main checkout and the other worktrees were verified unchanged afterwards. Test results are what each run reported; they were not re-run.
“Non-label text reworded” counts the helper text, footnote, Revert button, notice title and credits line. All six runs reworded the footnote.
Skill run 2 put its build folder beside its worktree instead of inside it. Nothing else left the worktrees.

The interface-text reference was written against the round-one failure on this very label, using an invented example from another domain. The slider result shows the fix works here; it does not show it generalises.
The kept and lost judgements and the key-difference notes are the evaluator's reading, not a measurement.
